title: Nvidia and IBM to Use AI to Correct Quantum Computing Errors, Paving Way for Practical Drug and Materials Discovery
excerpt: Nvidia and IBM, joined by the U.S. Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory, announced they will launch full-scale joint research to correct quantum…
content:
Nvidia and IBM will launch full-scale joint research to correct quantum computer calculation errors using artificial intelligence (AI) and GPUs. The two companies, alongside the U.S. Department of Energy's Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory, disclosed the research plan to coincide with SC26, an international supercomputing conference held in Chicago. The aim is to link quantum computing with conventional high-speed computing on the same equipment and tackle difficult scientific problems such as drug discovery and materials development.

Quantum computers use "qubits," basic units that can handle 0 and 1 simultaneously, and hold the potential to solve problems that conventional machines cannot solve in realistic time. However, errors arise easily from slight changes in the external environment, making quantum error correction—distributing information across multiple physical qubits to detect and fix errors—indispensable. This correction computation is enormous, and high-speed processing via GPUs is key.

In the joint research, a quantum computer equipped with IBM's "Nighthawk" quantum processor and Nvidia's AI computing system "DGX B200" will be placed side by side in the same facility and linked to each other. Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory will leverage knowledge cultivated in high-energy and nuclear physics research to participate in error correction and the design of next-generation computers. The two companies will also advance efforts to connect quantum processors to Slurm, the open-source software widely used for supercomputer job management. The goal is an environment where researchers can reserve and use quantum computing resources through the same operations they use to allocate CPUs and GPUs.

Nvidia also unveiled "TCBP-JOBS," an algorithm for quantum error correction research. In the company's tests, error decoding speed improved by up to 13,000x compared with major existing methods. It says the time required to study the design of a new quantum computer can be shortened from 12 weeks to 45 minutes. Note, however, that this is performance in a specific error-correction task; it does not mean the quantum computer itself became 13,000x faster at computation.

Demonstrations are also beginning to produce results. A research team from IBM, the Institute of Physical and Chemical Research, and Nvidia combined a quantum computer with GPUs to calculate the molecular structure of iron and sulfur contained in proteins and other substances in living organisms. According to IBM, calculation accuracy improved 79-fold compared with conventional experiments of the same kind. In separate research, the binding structure of a drug-discovery-related protein and a candidate compound was modeled at a scale of up to 12,635 atoms, and the work was selected as a finalist for the 2026 ACM Gordon Bell Prize.

Krista Svore, Nvidia's vice president of quantum computing application research, said, "To make quantum computers useful for science, progress is needed in everything—error correction, application fields, and the systems that connect quantum processors with high-speed computing," indicating that integrated hardware and software development is essential.

Science-Focused AI Models and CPU Platform Launched Together

Nvidia, not limiting itself to the quantum field, simultaneously announced a suite of AI models for scientific researchers, "Nemotron for Science," and the foundation for its high-performance computing CPU "Vera."

Nemotron is a family of AI models the company releases publicly, which companies and research institutions can further train for their own purposes. This time, "Nemotron 3.5 Super VL" was combined with chemical data and additional training methods, enabling it to read chemical reactions described in papers and draft experimental procedures, as well as support the design of proteins and drug candidate substances. A dataset containing about 50,000 questions for evaluating and training chemical reasoning, "LitmusBench v0.2," was also released, and the models and data are available on Hugging Face. They were optimized to run on-device even on the compact AI computer "DGX Spark," which carries 128 gigabytes of memory.

Use cases were also presented. Terray Therapeutics further trained the model to extract chemical reaction information from scientific figures and diagrams, identifying about 76% of the reactions described in test data. Biotech company Therna applied the model to the design of messenger RNA (mRNA) medicines, and the accuracy of predicting the range of protein expression levels reportedly nearly doubled compared with existing state-of-the-art models. The U.S. Argonne National Laboratory is incorporating Nemotron into multiple AI agents that design and evaluate protein candidates for treating cancer and other diseases.

On the computing infrastructure side, the company unveiled a Vera rack system equipped with 192 of its own designed CPUs. It features about 300 terabytes of memory and 1 petabyte of storage, with 88 cores and 176 threads per CPU, memory bandwidth of 1.2 terabytes per second, and more than 200 terabytes per second across the entire system. In the company's tests, fluid simulation performance was 1.9x that of x86-based systems and 2.4x in performance per watt. For weather forecasting models, it expects 1.6x performance and 2x energy efficiency. The German Climate Computing Center will adopt Vera for its next-generation supercomputer "HLRE-5," targeted to begin operation in early 2028.

Ian Buck, Nvidia's vice president, noted that "scientific simulation requires CPUs that can maintain performance while continuously moving large amounts of data," explaining that Vera eliminates the bottleneck between computation and data transfer. Vera-equipped racks are scheduled to ship from early 2027 through Dell, HPE, Lenovo, and Supermicro.

Benefits Born of Technological Convergence, and Preparations That Cannot Be Postponed

These announcements show that three technologies—quantum computing, AI, and high-speed computing—have entered a stage where they complement one another. GPUs and AI suppress errors in quantum computers, science-focused AI handles experiment planning and molecular design, and the CPU platform supports enormous simulations. Rather than a single technological innovation, the combination is making shorter timelines for drug discovery and materials exploration feel realistic.

On the other hand, the practical adoption of quantum computers also carries threats to existing encryption methods. Some of today's public-key cryptography could be broken once sufficiently powerful quantum computers emerge. There is also the pointed-out tactic of attackers collecting encrypted data first and storing it until the point when it can be decrypted, and companies and governments are being asked to migrate to post-quantum cryptography that is difficult even for quantum computers to break, and to grasp where within their organizations vulnerable cryptography is used.

Energy constraints also cannot be ignored. According to estimates published by the International Energy Agency (IEA) on November 19, 2026, data centers worldwide consumed just under 500 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025, accounting for 1.7% of global power demand. If current policies continue, data center power demand is projected to roughly double 2025 levels by 2030. The expansion of AI computing demand has entered a stage where computing infrastructure and power supply cannot be planned separately.

In the market, the focus is on how quickly the fusion of quantum computing and AI will translate into industrial applications. All the performance figures presented this time are results under limited operating conditions, and the timing for general-purpose quantum computers to reach practical use remains unclear. Still, it is significant that a design philosophy of tackling error correction—the biggest barrier to practical use—with GPUs and AI has been presented as concrete products and research plans. There may be a gap in competitiveness several years from now between companies that begin long-term preparations, including the allocation of computing resources, the cryptographic transition, and power procurement, and those that continue to wait and see.
